decoys.regime: prediction with many candidate predictors (p in the tens to thousands), any outcome
decoys.statement: Complementary-pairs stability selection with B = 50 pairs of random halves, each half's first q variables on the lasso path, threshold tau = 0.6 and q = floor((2*tau - 1)*p) keeps the expected number of falsely selected predictors at or below 1, by Meinshausen & Bühlmann's bound q^2/((2*tau - 1)p), which complementary pairs keep under the same exchangeability assumption.
decoys.claimed_basis: variable_selection.py:57-59; Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2010 Thm 1; Shah & Samworth 2013 (JRSS B 75:55); tau at the lower end of (0.6, 0.9).
decoys.why_false: With q = floor((2tau-1)p) the bound q^2/((2tau-1)p) equals about (2tau-1)p = 0.2p, which exceeds 1 for p > 5; the bound is at most 1 only with q <= sqrt((2tau-1)p).

decoys.regime: yes/no outcome whose rarer class is below 20% of rows, prediction
decoys.statement: For a yes/no outcome whose rarer class is below 20% of rows, random oversampling or SMOTE of the rarer class should be applied by default inside each training fold, because it raises the AUC and corrects the model's tendency to underestimate the rarer class's probability, so the decision threshold can stay at 0.5.
decoys.claimed_basis: van den Goorbergh et al., JAMIA 2022;29:1525.
decoys.why_false: van den Goorbergh et al. 2022 found that imbalance corrections did not improve AUC and made the rarer class's probabilities overestimated (miscalibration); the fix for a decision is moving the threshold, not resampling.

decoys.regime: comparing two families' cross-validated scores on a repeated k-fold substrate (10 × 5), any outcome
decoys.statement: For the difference between two families' cross-validated scores on 10 repeats of 5 folds, the ordinary paired t on the rK − 1 = 49 degrees of freedom over the 50 fold differences, t = mean(d)/√(s²_d/(rK)), gives an approximately valid 95% interval, because repeating the folds 10 times makes the fold differences approximately independent.
decoys.claimed_basis: RECIPES §3.7 comparison table; Dietterich 1998 (Neural Computation 10:1895); Bouckaert & Frank, PAKDD 2004.
decoys.why_false: Fold differences share training rows and are positively correlated; the naive paired t is anti-conservative (inflated type I error), which is why Nadeau & Bengio's corrected variance (1/(rK) + n2/n1)s² is used. Repeating does not make them independent.

decoys.regime: any goal (describe, estimate or predict) with blanks in predictors
decoys.statement: Including the outcome in the imputation model is invalid under every goal, including estimating a regression coefficient, because the outcome would then inform its own predictors and bias the coefficients away from zero; blanks in predictors must always be imputed without the outcome.
decoys.claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 (blanks); Sisk et al. 2023; BLUEPRINT §12 ruling 4.
decoys.why_false: For estimation, the outcome must be in the imputation model; omitting it biases coefficients toward zero (Moons et al. 2006, J Clin Epidemiol; Sterne et al. 2009, BMJ). The exclusion is specific to deployment-time prediction.

decoys.regime: inference with repeated rows per unit, about 12 units
decoys.statement: Under inference with repeated units, GEE with an exchangeable working correlation and the ordinary sandwich variance (CR0) with a normal reference gives near-nominal type I error even with about 12 units, so no small-sample correction of the sandwich is needed.
decoys.why_false: With few clusters the CR0 sandwich is biased downward and z intervals are anti-conservative (Mancl & DeRouen 2001; Cameron & Miller 2015 recommend small-sample corrections and t(G−1) references).

decoys.regime: estimation with a two-valued covariate that is a declared modifier (in an interaction with the exposure)
decoys.statement: Under Estimate, relabeling a two-valued column that is a declared modifier of the exposure (in an exposure × modifier interaction), coding its two spellings the other way round, leaves the exposure's main coefficient and its interval exactly unchanged and only flips the sign of the modifier's own coefficient and the interaction term, so the repair needs no post-lock check.
decoys.claimed_basis: materiality_calibration.json 'invariance' entry; SURFACING_POLICY §2.6; Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (Frisch & Waugh 1933; Lovell 1963).
decoys.why_false: With an interaction, the exposure's main coefficient is its slope at the modifier's reference level; swapping the coding changes the reference level, so the main coefficient becomes the other group's slope (beta + gamma) and its interval changes.

decoys.regime: unpenalized logistic regression under prediction
decoys.decision: predictor scaling for unpenalized logistic regression
decoys.statement: For an unpenalized logistic regression fit by maximum likelihood, multiplying any predictor by a positive constant before fitting leaves the out-of-fold predicted probabilities unchanged, so the app does not rescale predictors for this family.
decoys.claimed_basis: Equivariance of the maximum-likelihood estimate under linear reparameterization (McCullagh & Nelder 1989).
decoys.why_false: TRUE but vacuous: the natural alternative (rescaling) gives identical predictions, so the claim changes no decision or result (bite = no).

decoys.regime: random forest under prediction
decoys.statement: The random forest's standard settings — 500 trees, each on a bootstrap of every row, mtry floor(p/3) for a class outcome and floor(√p) for a numeric outcome — are randomForest's and ranger's documented defaults.
decoys.why_false: randomForest's defaults are mtry = floor(√p) for classification and max(floor(p/3), 1) for regression; ranger's default is floor(√p) for both. The decoy's class default p/3 matches neither package, and its numeric default √p is not randomForest's.

decoys.regime: prediction on complex survey data (strata, PSUs, weights), population performance wanted
decoys.statement: Under prediction on survey data with weights, ordinary unweighted K-fold cross-validation with folds drawn at random over rows estimates the surveyed population's performance without bias, because randomly drawn folds are themselves simple random samples of the design.
decoys.claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 13; Wieczorek, Guerin & McMahon, Stat 2022;11:e454.
decoys.why_false: Unweighted CV estimates performance on the sample's composition, not the population's; with informative weights it is biased for population performance, and row-level folds split PSUs. Wieczorek et al. 2022 propose design-based CV precisely because of this.

decoys.regime: NHANES analyses combining exam, fasting-subsample and dietary variables
decoys.statement: For NHANES data the correct survey weight is the weight of the largest sample on which any analysis variable was measured — the MEC examination weight whenever an examination variable is in the model, even when a fasting analyte such as glucose is also analyzed — because it keeps the most participants and so gives the most precise estimate.
decoys.why_false: The NHANES tutorial says to use the weight of the smallest subpopulation that includes all variables (e.g., the fasting subsample weight for fasting glucose); the MEC weight does not represent the population for subsample-only variables.

decoys.regime: untargeted metabolomics with pooled QC samples
decoys.statement: A feature whose D-ratio (pooled-QC SD over the study samples' SD) is 50% or less carries too little biological variance relative to technical variance and is removed, with the QC SD frozen before the seal and the study SD taken from each training fold.
decoys.why_false: Direction reversed: a LOW D-ratio means technical variance is small relative to biological variance (a good feature); Broadhurst et al. keep features with D-ratio below 50% and remove those at or above.

decoys.regime: nutrition exposure–outcome analysis, cross-sectional or cohort
decoys.statement: In a nutrition exposure–outcome analysis, any covariate associated with both the exposure and the outcome in the data, including BMI and blood pressure measured at the same visit, belongs in the adjustment set as a confounder, since association with both is the criterion for confounding.
decoys.why_false: Association with both is not the criterion: mediators (BMI on the path from diet to outcome) and colliders are associated with both and adjusting for them biases the total effect. VanderWeele 2019's disjunctive cause criterion is about causes, measured pre-exposure.

decoys.regime: inference with values below a detection limit
decoys.statement: Under inference, substituting half the feature's minimum for values below detection is acceptable while QRILC is refused, because a deterministic fill adds no imputation uncertainty, so the intervals computed afterwards remain valid.
decoys.why_false: A deterministic single fill ignores the uncertainty of the unknown values and distorts variances and regression estimates; intervals are too narrow and estimates can be biased. Helsel 2006 argues against substitution for exactly this reason.

decoys.regime: yes/no outcome, held-out validation
decoys.decision: minimum size of a held-out set
decoys.statement: For a yes/no outcome, a held-out validation set with at least 10 events estimates the C-statistic and the calibration slope precisely enough to be useful, so a held-out score is offered from 10 events.
decoys.why_false: Collins et al. 2016 found validation studies need a minimum of about 100 events (preferably 200 or more) for precise calibration and discrimination estimates; 10 events gives very wide, unstable estimates.

decoys.regime: least-squares fit on any table
decoys.decision: row order before a least-squares fit
decoys.statement: Sorting or permuting the rows of a table before an ordinary least-squares fit leaves its coefficients, intervals and fitted values unchanged, so the app does not shuffle rows before a least-squares fit.
decoys.claimed_basis: Invariance of X'X and X'y to row permutation.
decoys.why_false: TRUE but vacuous: shuffling or not changes nothing, so the claim governs no decision (bite = no).

decoys.regime: prediction with many candidate predictors, internal validation
decoys.statement: Under prediction, steps that never use the outcome (scaling, PCA loadings, median imputation) must be fit inside each training fold, but screening predictors by their univariate association with the outcome may be done once on all rows before cross-validation without biasing the error estimate, because the screen uses only each predictor's marginal association.
decoys.why_false: Reversed: outcome-based screening on all rows before CV is the classic leak and gives badly optimistic error (Ambroise & McLachlan 2002; ESL §7.10.2 'the wrong way'). Unsupervised steps are the ones that cause little bias.

decoys.regime: internal validation at typical clinical sample sizes (hundreds to a few thousand rows)
decoys.statement: For internal validation at typical clinical sample sizes, a single random 70/30 train/test split is the recommended default, because it gives a less biased and more precise estimate of performance than bootstrap optimism correction or repeated cross-validation.
decoys.claimed_basis: CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK §A5.5 (CONVENTION); Steyerberg et al. 2001 (J Clin Epidemiol 54:774).
decoys.why_false: Steyerberg et al. 2001 found split-sample validation inefficient and imprecise, and recommended bootstrap optimism correction; a single split is the weakest option at these sizes.

decoys.regime: longitudinal exposure with a time-varying confounder affected by earlier exposure
decoys.statement: When a time-varying confounder was itself affected by earlier exposure, a standard regression that adjusts for the confounder at every time point gives an unbiased estimate of the total effect of the exposure history, so marginal structural models are needed only to gain efficiency.
decoys.why_false: Adjusting for a confounder that is also a mediator of earlier exposure blocks part of the effect and can open collider paths; standard regression is biased whether or not it adjusts (Robins et al. 2000), which is why MSMs or g-methods are needed for unbiasedness, not efficiency.

decoys.regime: population survey design (strata, PSUs), subgroup analysis
decoys.decision: subgroup analysis under a survey design
decoys.statement: Under a population survey design, a subgroup analysis should first delete the rows outside the subgroup and then compute Taylor-linearized variances, because keeping them would let PSUs with no subgroup members inflate the subgroup's standard error.
decoys.why_false: Reversed: deleting rows can drop PSUs and strata from the variance calculation and gives incorrect standard errors; the guidelines say to keep all rows and use a domain (subpopulation) indicator.

decoys.regime: regression outcome under prediction, cross-validated or held-out scoring
decoys.statement: Under Predict, the cross-validated R² for a regression outcome is best reported as the squared Pearson correlation between the out-of-fold predictions and the outcomes, because it penalizes predictions that are systematically too high or too low and so is the conservative choice over 1 − SSE/SST.
decoys.why_false: The squared correlation is invariant to any affine transformation of the predictions, so it does not penalize a systematic shift or scale error at all; it is optimistic relative to 1 − SSE/SST, which does (and can go below zero). Kvålseth 1985 warns against the squared-correlation form for this reason.

decoys.regime: internal–external cross-validation across survey cycles (k cycles), heterogeneous performance
decoys.statement: Internal–external cross-validation across survey cycles is summarized by a fixed-effect inverse-variance meta-analysis of each cycle's MSE with a normal 95% interval, which also serves as a valid prediction interval for a new cycle's MSE when cycles' performance is heterogeneous.
decoys.claimed_basis: Riley et al. 2016 (BMJ 353:i3140); Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter 2009.
decoys.why_false: A fixed-effect confidence interval for the mean is not a prediction interval for a new cycle under heterogeneity; the prediction interval needs the between-cycle variance (random effects, t(k−2)), as Riley et al. 2011/2016 and Higgins et al. 2009 state.

decoys.regime: regression outcome under prediction, comparing families by pooled cross-validated error
decoys.decision: score shown in the comparison table
decoys.statement: Under Predict, showing the pooled cross-validated root mean squared error instead of the mean squared error never changes which family has the lower score, because the square root is increasing, so the comparison table can show either.
decoys.why_false: TRUE but vacuous: the ranking is identical either way, so the choice changes no decision (bite = no).

decoys.regime: randomized trial with non-adherence
decoys.statement: In a randomized trial the primary analysis is per protocol: only participants who received the assigned treatment as planned, analyzed in that arm, because excluding non-adherers removes noise while the comparison stays protected by randomization.
decoys.why_false: Excluding by post-randomization adherence breaks the protection randomization gives (adherers differ from non-adherers); intention to treat is the primary analysis, and CONSORT item 16 asks for the analysis by original assigned groups.

decoys.regime: describing usual intake from one or two 24-hour recalls per person
decoys.statement: The distribution of each person's mean of two 24-hour recalls is narrower than the distribution of usual (long-run average) intake, because averaging two days pulls each person toward the population mean, so percentiles read from it understate the share in both tails.
decoys.claimed_basis: NUTRITION_PACK §03; Tooze et al. 2006 (J Am Diet Assoc 106:1575).
decoys.why_false: Reversed: the mean of two days still carries within-person variance (σ²_w/2) on top of between-person variance, so its distribution is WIDER than usual intake's and overstates both tails; Tooze et al.'s NCI method removes that extra variance.

decoys.regime: dietary exposure, energy adjustment, non-linear dose–response
decoys.decision: energy model for a curved exposure
decoys.statement: The residual energy model and the standard (nutrient plus energy) model give the same nutrient effect for any functional form, so a restricted cubic spline of the energy residual estimates the nutrient's substitution curve at fixed total energy exactly as a spline of the nutrient with energy beside it does.
decoys.claimed_basis: Willett, Howe & Kushi 1997 (Am J Clin Nutr 65:1220S).
decoys.why_false: The equivalence holds for a straight line only (by Frisch–Waugh–Lovell); a spline of the residual is a curve on the energy-adjusted scale at mean energy, not the substitution curve at fixed energy, and the two curves differ in general.

decoys.regime: cluster-randomized trial with few clusters (K under 40), GEE
decoys.decision: degrees of freedom for GEE intervals
decoys.statement: GEE intervals in a cluster-randomized trial use a t reference on the number of participants minus 2 degrees of freedom (intercept and arm), since each participant contributes one residual to the sandwich variance.
decoys.why_false: With few clusters the sandwich's effective information comes from clusters, not participants; Li & Redden 2015 recommend t on K − 2 (clusters minus cluster-level parameters), and participant-based df gives anti-conservative intervals.

decoys.regime: individually matched case-control study, predicting absolute risk
decoys.decision: absolute risk prediction from a matched case-control design
decoys.statement: Absolute risks can be predicted from individually matched case-control sets by fitting conditional logistic regression and adding the log of the control sampling fraction to the model's intercept, which recalibrates the sample's odds to the population's.
decoys.why_false: Conditional logistic regression has no intercept (each matched set's intercept is conditioned away), and matched controls are not a random sample of non-cases, so no single offset recovers absolute risk; the Prentice–Pyke offset applies to unmatched designs with known sampling fractions.

decoys.regime: sensitivity to unmeasured confounding for a risk ratio above 1
decoys.statement: For an observed risk ratio RR above 1, the E-value is RR + √(RR − 1), so a risk ratio of 2 has an E-value of 3: an unmeasured confounder would need risk ratios of 3 with both exposure and outcome to explain it away.
decoys.why_false: The E-value is RR + √(RR × (RR − 1)); for RR = 2 it is 2 + √2 ≈ 3.41, not 3.

decoys.regime: inference on a continuous dietary exposure
decoys.decision: functional form of a continuous exposure
decoys.statement: Under inference, quintiles of a continuous exposure estimate its dose–response as efficiently as a restricted cubic spline and without its modeling assumptions, so they rank above the spline as the primary form.
decoys.claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 2; NUTRITION_PACK §07G; Royston, Altman & Sauerbrei 2006 (Stat Med 25:127).
decoys.why_false: Categorizing a continuous exposure loses information and power and assumes steps at arbitrary cuts; Royston, Altman & Sauerbrei 2006 ('Dichotomizing continuous predictors in multiple regression: a bad idea') argue against it, and splines are more efficient.

decoys.regime: least-squares model under inference
decoys.decision: order of predictors in the model
decoys.statement: Under inference, the order in which predictors are listed in a least-squares model does not change the exposure's coefficient, interval or p-value (only sequential sums of squares depend on order, and the app does not report them), so the app does not ask about predictor order.
decoys.claimed_basis: Invariance of the least-squares solution to column permutation.
decoys.why_false: TRUE but vacuous: the order changes no reported number, so the claim governs no decision (bite = no).

dropped_dupes.why: the same energy-screen 'doesn't change your numbers' cutoff (0.003697), inventoried in A and C; both agents put it in their suspect lists
the same complete-case 'only if missingness does not depend on the outcome' claim, inventoried in B and D; both agents put it in their suspect lists
the same NHANES 'smallest subsample weight' rule, both in the random sample
the same design-based survey cross-validation rule, both in C's random sample
